a: When Jehoiakim son of Josiah had just become king of Judah
p: Josiah had just died at Megiddo; his son Jehoiakim ruled as Egypt's choice.
b: Josiah was killed at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29). The people crowned his son Jehoahaz, but Pharaoh Necho removed him after three months and set up Jehoiakim, an older half-brother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31, 36 give their ages at accession as 23 and 25), as his vassal (2 Kings 23:30–35). Chapter 26 therefore opens in the first months of a king who was hostile to prophets and loyal to Egypt. The chapter's story of Uriah (26:20–23) shows how far that loyalty reached. The Hebrew heading says "Jehoiakim" here without any difficulty; the matching heading at 27:1 is the one that is disputed (see there).

a: Stand in the courtyard of the LORD's house
p: Chapter 26 tells what happened after a Temple sermon; chapter 7 gives its text.
b: Jeremiah 7:1–15 reports a Temple-gate sermon that also warns of a fate like Shiloh's (7:12–14). Many scholars take chapter 7 as the sermon and chapter 26 as the story of its aftermath, told by a different hand (the "Baruch" source, in Mowinckel's scheme). Others think the two are separate occasions, since chapter 7 has no trial and chapter 26 contains only the shorter warning of 26:4–6. A third view holds that chapter 7 expands what chapter 26 sums up. Either way, chapter 26 shows the cost of the words in chapter 7. The "Plain" here follows the Hebrew order and does not merge the two.

a: change my mind
t: The LORD changes his mind, and the pun on "evil"
p: Nicham and ra'ah: the LORD can turn from "the evil" he planned if they turn from their "evil."
b: The verb is nicham, "be sorry, change one's mind." The Hebrew uses one word, ra'ah (evil, harm), both for the people's deeds and for the harm God plans, so "evil way" and "evil planned" sound alike. English needs two words, so the Plain says "harm" for God's judgment and "evil" or "wicked" for the people's acts. The verse turns on shuv (turn back): if they turn back, he will turn from his plan. The same teaching is in 18:7–10, and Jonah 3:10 is the best-known case. It does not mean God is fickle; the threat was a warning meant to be avoided.

a: my law
p: Here torah means the law God set before the people, which they would not follow.
b: Torah means "teaching" or "instruction," and for Jeremiah's hearers it meant the Teaching of Moses, perhaps the "book of the law" found in Josiah's reform (2 Kings 22:8). The Plain uses "law" when the command to "walk" in it points to rules for life. Jeremiah quotes the same charge at 9:13 and 32:23. The picture is of a road God "set in front of" the people (Deuteronomy 11:26; 30:15). The word returns in the promise of a law written on the heart (31:33).

a: like Shiloh
p: Shiloh housed the ark before David. Jeremiah said the Temple could fall the same way.
b: Shiloh, in the hills of Ephraim, held the tent shrine and the ark in the days of Eli and Samuel (1 Samuel 1–4). After the ark was captured, the shrine ceased to be the center of worship, and Psalm 78:60 says God abandoned it. Jeremiah used it as proof that a holy place does not protect a people who ignore the LORD (also 7:12–14; 26:9). Excavators at Shiloh (the Danish expedition, and in the 1980s Israel Finkelstein's) have reported a destruction layer from about 1050 BC; whether the Philistines caused it is debated, and the site was lived in thinly in later periods, so how Jeremiah's hearers pictured Shiloh's ruin is also debated. The audience in 609 BC trusted Jerusalem's Temple as unbreakable (compare 7:4), and Isaiah's earlier saving of Jerusalem in 701 BC (Isaiah 37) may have strengthened that trust.

a: a word that every nation on earth uses to curse
p: The city would become an example people name when they wish someone the same fate.
b: The Hebrew is "I will make this city into a curse (qelalah) for all the nations of the earth." A curse of this kind names a famous disaster: people would say, "May the LORD make you like Jerusalem." Jeremiah gives the pattern itself in 29:22 ("May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab"). It is the opposite of the blessing promised to Abraham, in which nations bless themselves by Abraham's offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). The Plain spells the image out so English readers do not think the city is only being insulted.

a: You will certainly die!
t: The charge of a death-sentence prophecy
p: Mot tamut is the language of capital law; the law named death for a false prophet.
b: Mot tamut ("dying you will die") is the form used in the Torah for crimes that carry the death penalty (Exodus 21:12; Leviticus 20:9). Deuteronomy ordered death for a prophet who spoke in the LORD's name what he had not been told to say, or who called people to other gods (Deuteronomy 18:20; 13:5). The priests and prophets accuse Jeremiah on that ground (26:9, 11), and he answers by claiming he really was sent (26:12, 15). The scene is the Bible's clearest trial of a prophet before Jesus and Stephen (Matthew 26:59–66; Acts 6:11–14).

a: the New Gate of the LORD's house
t: The New Gate and the court of officials
p: The officials came up from the palace and held court at a Temple gate.
b: The palace stood just south of the Temple on the same hill, so the officials "came up" to the Temple. City gates were the place where elders and judges heard cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2), and the Temple gate played the same role here. The New Gate is also named in 36:10, where Baruch reads Jeremiah's scroll from a room beside it. The officials (sarim) are royal court officers, not priests, and they act as the judges. Their verdict goes against the priests and prophets who brought the charge.

a: This man has earned a death sentence
p: The accusers are the priests and prophets of the Temple, and the accusation is political as well as religious.
b: The Hebrew is literally "a sentence of death belongs to this man" (mishpat-mavet). The speakers are the priests and the prophets, the people whose standing depended on the Temple. Jeremiah was himself a priest's son (1:1), so this is a quarrel inside the priesthood. The charge is that he "prophesied against this city" (26:11), which could be heard as treason against the king as well as blasphemy. The Greek calls the prophets "false prophets" here and in 26:7, 8 and 16 (see the variant at 26:8).

a: innocent blood
p: Shedding the blood of someone who has done no wrong stains the land and everyone in it.
b: In the Torah, spilling innocent blood put guilt on the whole community until it was dealt with (Deuteronomy 19:10; 21:1–9). The Bible blames Manasseh for filling Jerusalem with innocent blood, and says this was why the LORD would not forgive Judah (2 Kings 21:16; 24:4). Jeremiah uses the idea twice more in his own sermons (7:6; 22:3, 17). Here he gives the judges a plain warning: killing him would make the sin of Manasseh's day their own.
r: Deuteronomy 19:10; Deuteronomy 21:1–9; 2 Kings 21:16; 2 Kings 24:4; Jeremiah 7:6; Jeremiah 22:17

a: Micah of Moresheth
t: Micah is quoted as a precedent
p: The elders cite Micah 3:12, the only place a prophet's earlier words are quoted by name and date.
b: Micah's book opens in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), and 3:12 contains the words the elders quote. This is the only time in the prophets that an earlier prophet's saying is cited by name, with a king's reign, as legal precedent. The Hebrew text spells the name Mikayah (Micaiah) in the written text and Mikah (Micah) in the reading tradition (Ketiv and Qere); it is the same man. Moresheth (Moresheth-gath, Micah 1:14) lay in the Judean foothills about 25 miles southwest of Jerusalem. The Plain of Micah will follow this wording where the Hebrew is the same.

a: high ground in a forest
p: The Temple hill becomes bare high ground overgrown with brush, not a sacred high place.
b: The Hebrew is bamot ya'ar, literally "high places of a forest." Bamah is the usual word for a hilltop shrine, which gives the line a sting: the mountain of the house would be a "high place" only in the sense of a wooded hill. Jeremiah's hearers would hear the contrast with the Temple Mount, the place the LORD chose. Micah 3:12 uses the same Hebrew; the Plain of Micah will be worded to match.

a: beg the LORD for mercy
p: A Hebrew idiom for begging a favor; Hezekiah's fear and prayer turned the judgment aside.
b: The idiom is chillah et-penei YHWH, "soften (or sweeten) the face of the LORD." It is used for pleading with a king or with God (Exodus 32:11; 1 Kings 13:6). The Bible says Hezekiah humbled himself and the LORD's anger did not come in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). The elders turn this into a lesson: Micah warned, the king listened, and the harm did not come. They also change the plan of the court from "Is he guilty?" to "What did Hezekiah do?" The "change of mind" is the same verb as in 26:3, so the elders show they have heard Jeremiah's message.

a: Uriah son of Shemaiah
t: Uriah, the prophet who was killed
p: A second prophet with Jeremiah's message, killed on the king's orders; found only here.
b: Uriah appears only in this passage. He came from Kiriath-jearim, a town west of Jerusalem where the ark had once been kept (1 Samuel 7:1–2), and preached "just like Jeremiah." King Jehoiakim, Necho's vassal (2 Kings 23:34), could ask Egypt to hand him over. The story is placed after Jeremiah's rescue (26:16–19) as a warning: Jeremiah's escape was not guaranteed. It also shows Jehoiakim's character, which Jeremiah later describes (22:13–19; 36:23).

a: Elnathan son of Achbor
t: Elnathan, an official who knew the prophet
p: The same man later pleads with the king not to burn Jeremiah's scroll.
b: Elnathan son of Achbor served as the king's agent here. Achbor had been among Josiah's men sent to the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12–14). In 36:12, 25 Elnathan is one of the officials who hears Baruch read the scroll and urges the king not to burn it. Jehoiachin's mother Nehushta was a daughter of an Elnathan of Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8), and some identify him with this man. If the Elnathan of 36:12, 25 is the same man, the text shows an official who carried out a killing and yet later spoke up for the prophet's book; the Bible does not say they are one person. Lachish Letter 3, from the same years, names a Konyahu son of Elnathan, so the name was in use in more than one family. The Greek leaves out his name (see the variant).

a: burial ground of the common people
p: The "graves of the sons of the people" were the common burial ground, not a family tomb.
b: Kings and nobles were buried in family tombs (2 Kings 21:18; 23:30). The "graves of the common people" were a public burial ground by the Kidron Valley, where Josiah had scattered the ashes of the Asherah (2 Kings 23:6). Throwing Uriah's body there showed contempt. Jehoiakim's own end was foretold in a similar form: he would be buried like a donkey (22:19).

a: Ahikam son of Shaphan stood by Jeremiah
p: A powerful family at court protected Jeremiah, and its members appear across the book.
b: Shaphan was Josiah's secretary, who read the newly found law to the king (2 Kings 22:3–14). His sons Ahikam, Elasah (29:3) and Gemariah (36:10–12) and his grandson Gedaliah (39:14; 40:5) all appear in Jeremiah's story, usually on his side. "The hand of Ahikam was with Jeremiah" is an idiom for support and protection. Ahikam's help here and the elders' appeal (26:17–19) together explain why a man who spoke what the court found treasonous was not killed in 609 BC.

a: When Zedekiah son of Josiah had just become king of Judah
t: A date that does not fit: Zedekiah's accession or his fourth year
p: The heading puts the word at the start of Zedekiah's reign, but 28:1 dates the same events to his fourth year.
b: The Hebrew heading says bereshit mamlekhet, "in the beginning of the reign," and names Jehoiakim; the Plain reads Zedekiah (see the variant). The tension with the date in 28:1, "in the fourth year," is inherited from the Hebrew: 28:1 itself says "early in the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year." Some take "beginning of the reign" loosely, as the early years of a reign that lasted eleven; others take the heading as a copy of 26:1. The chapter's own details (the envoys, the objects taken with Jeconiah in 597 BC) fit Zedekiah's fourth year, about 594/593 BC.

a: straps and yoke-bars
p: Jeremiah acts out the message: Judah must carry Babylon's yoke.
b: A yoke is the wooden beam that joins oxen to a plow or cart; in the ancient world it was also a common picture of conquest and tribute (1 Kings 12:4; Isaiah 10:27). The Hebrew moserot (straps, ties) and motot (yoke-bars, poles) name the harness. Jeremiah's wearing of it is a sign-act, like the linen belt of 13:1–11, the broken jar of 19:1–11 and the sign-acts of Isaiah 20:2–4 and Ezekiel 4. In the Qumran copy 4QJer-c (4Q72), motot (yoke-bars) is preserved and moserot (straps) is restored by the editors, so the scroll shows no difference from the Hebrew; the Greek has "bonds and collars." Chapter 28 shows people reading the yoke as a political statement, not only a symbol.

a: by the messengers who have come to Jerusalem
p: Five neighbors sent envoys to Zedekiah; the text does not say why, and a plan to revolt against Babylon is the common guess.
b: Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon are the same five nations named in the cup of wrath (25:21–22). Their envoys came to Jerusalem in the fourth year of Zedekiah, about 594/593 BC (28:1). The text says only that the envoys had come. Many historians link the visit to unrest in Babylon itself: the Babylonian Chronicle reports a revolt in Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year (595/594 BC), which may have given smaller kingdoms hope that his hold was weakening. Others look to Egypt, where Psamtik II (reigned 595–589 BC) was taking an interest in the region. Either way, the link to a planned revolt is a historians' hypothesis. Jeremiah's message is that the hope is false: God has given these lands to Babylon. 51:59 says that Zedekiah went to Babylon in his fourth year; the reason is not given, and some propose that he went to prove his loyalty.

a: send them to the king of Edom
t: "Send them": the yokes themselves go out
p: The Hebrew and the Greek say "send them": the yokes are sent to the five kings.
b: The Hebrew is veshillachtam, "and you will send them," and the "them" can only be the straps and yoke-bars of 27:2. The Greek has "you will send them" (Greek 34:2), and 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves the word in 27:3. So the sign-act is not only worn but delivered: the yokes go to the five kings. Some commentators read the suffix as the message ("send word"), and that is the older English wording, but the Hebrew and Greek both have a plain object pronoun after a verb of sending, and the yokes are the only thing in the context to send. The Plain follows the Hebrew with the Greek and the scroll.

a: by my great strength and my outstretched arm
p: The LORD claims the earth, and so the right to assign it to Babylon.
b: "Great strength and outstretched arm" is the Exodus phrase (Deuteronomy 4:34; 5:15; 9:29) and also stands in Jeremiah's own prayer at 32:17, where it describes creation. Here it is a claim of authority. The God of Israel made the earth and gives it "to anyone I think right," so a pagan empire holds its rule by his permission. The same lesson is taught to Nebuchadnezzar himself in Daniel 4:17, 25, 32. For the envoys of Edom and Moab, who had their own national gods, it is a bold claim.

a: my servant
p: The LORD calls a pagan king his servant, as he calls Cyrus his shepherd and anointed.
b: The Hebrew eved means "servant" or "slave" by context. Applied to Nebuchadnezzar it means a tool in God's hand, not a believer: compare 25:9 and 43:10, and "Cyrus, my shepherd" and "his anointed" in Isaiah 44:28; 45:1. The title shocked those who thought God's servants were Israel and David. The Greek text printed by Swete does not have "my servant" in this verse. The same verse says the wild animals will serve him (Daniel 2:38 uses nearly the same phrase of him).

a: his son, and his son's son
p: The words may be literal, or a round number for a short dynasty; the Greek lacks the verse.
b: Nebuchadnezzar ruled 605–562 BC. His son Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach, 2 Kings 25:27) reigned two years, and after a short series of rulers, Nabonidus (556–539 BC), who was not Nebuchadnezzar's descendant, was king when Cyrus took the city. Some read "his son and his son's son" as a fixed expression for "a few generations" ; others take it as a literal forecast; critics who think the verse is a later addition (the Greek lacks it) say it was written when the dynasty's end was in sight. Daniel 5 calls Belshazzar "son" of Nebuchadnezzar. The end of his "own land's time" is the fall of Babylon in 539 BC.

a: your dreams
p: Prophets, diviners, dreams, fortune-tellers and sorcerers: the list echoes the Torah's ban on divination.
b: The five groups echo Deuteronomy 18:10–11, which forbids a list of diviners, and Deuteronomy 13:1–5, which warns about "a dreamer of dreams." The Hebrew text says "your dreams" (chalomoteikhem), and the Greek says "your dreamers" (people who dream), a likely smoother reading; the Plain follows the Hebrew. These were the usual ways a king like Zedekiah looked for advice, and the five envoys would have used them too. Jeremiah's point is that they all give the same answer, "You will not serve Babylon," and all of them are wrong.

a: prophesying a lie
p: Sheqer runs through chapters 27–29: the prophets of peace speak falsehood in the LORD's name.
b: Sheqer ("lie, falsehood") is Jeremiah's word for the false prophets' message and for the way people trust it. It occurs in nine verses of this section (27:10, 14, 15, 16; 28:15; 29:9, 21, 23, 31) and earlier in 5:2; 6:13; 8:10; 14:14; 23:25–26. The lie is not only a wrong prediction. It is a false use of the LORD's name ("in my name"), and its result is exile. The Greek of this chapter often uses words for "unjust" or "false" in place of one standard word. The purpose word in 27:10 and 27:15 is lema'an, "in order that"; many English versions soften it to a result. The Plain keeps the purpose: the lie works to remove the people from their land, and the Greek of 27:10 says the same (pros to makrynai, "so as to remove"). The prophets did not intend exile; the sentence says what their message in fact serves.

a: Serve him and his people, and live
p: Jeremiah told the king to submit to Babylon; to some he was disloyal, to others a faithful prophet.
b: In the eyes of the war party, advice to surrender sounded like treason, and the officials later said as much (38:2–4). Jeremiah's reasons were religious: Babylon was God's tool (27:6), and resistance would cost lives and the city. Commentators stress that this is not praise of Babylon or a call to pacifism in general, since Jeremiah elsewhere announces Babylon's own fall (25:12; 50–51), and some see it as realism about Babylon's strength. The gift of "live" appears also in 21:9 and 38:17–18.

a: the objects of the LORD's house
t: The Temple vessels taken in 597 BC
p: Part of the Temple treasure went to Babylon in 597; more would go in 586.
b: In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar carried off Jehoiachin and took treasures and gold vessels from the Temple and the palace (2 Kings 24:13; 2 Chronicles 36:10; Daniel 1:2). The prophets of peace said they would be back "very soon." Jeremiah says the opposite: what remains will go too. The Babylonians broke up and removed the rest in 586 (2 Kings 25:13–17; Jeremiah 52:17–23). They came back only under Cyrus, who gave 5,400 vessels to Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:7–11).

a: let them plead with the LORD of Armies
p: Prophets were meant to intercede; here the false prophets are told to prove themselves by prayer.
b: A true prophet speaks to the people for God and also to God for the people. Moses and Samuel were the model intercessors (Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23), and Jeremiah himself was told not to intercede for Judah (7:16; 11:14; 14:11; compare 15:1, "Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me..."). Here Jeremiah turns the test around: if the prophets of peace really have the LORD's word, let them pray to keep the remaining vessels from going. The challenge implies they cannot.
r: Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23; Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1

a: the pillars, the Sea, the stands
t: The great bronze furniture of the Temple
p: Two pillars, the bronze Sea (a huge basin) and ten wheeled stands were Solomon's work.
b: Solomon had them cast in bronze: the two pillars Jakin and Boaz, the huge basin called the Sea, and ten wheeled stands for water basins (1 Kings 7:15–39). They were too heavy to carry off in 597 BC. In 586 the Babylonians broke them up and took the bronze (2 Kings 25:13, 16; Jeremiah 52:17–20). Jeremiah is saying that even the most solid parts of the Temple would be taken. The Greek text has only a short summary of 27:19–22 (see the variants).

a: until the day I call for them
p: The vessels would stay in Babylon until the LORD turned his attention to them again.
b: The Hebrew verb is paqad, "visit, take notice of, call to account," the same verb as in 29:10 ("I will turn my attention to you"). It can mean judgment or rescue. Here it promises return, and the Bible shows the return in Ezra 1:7–11 and 5:14–15, under Cyrus, long after the dispute with Hananiah. The belief that the vessels would come back is therefore both true and, in the shape given by Hananiah, wrong: the return was in God's time, not in two years. Daniel 5:2–4 shows Babylon's kings using the vessels at a feast before the empire fell.

a: Hananiah son of Azzur, a man from Gibeon
p: A prophet from a priestly town; the book gives him no other record.
b: Hananiah is named only here. Gibeon, a few miles northwest of Jerusalem, was one of the towns assigned to the descendants of Aaron (Joshua 21:17–18), as Anathoth was (Jeremiah 1:1). The two men who clash in the Temple may therefore both come from priestly families. The book calls him "the prophet" again and again, which is how the text names his office even when it shows him wrong. The Greek calls him "the false prophet" (pseudoprophetes) at the start, and it does the same for the other prophets in chapters 26–29.

a: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon
t: A promise in the past tense
p: Hananiah speaks as if the thing is already done; the verb form is the "prophetic perfect."
b: Shavarti is a perfect tense, "I have broken." Prophets often used the past tense for a promise they were sure of, as if it had already happened. Hananiah's boast is bold; then in 28:4 he changes to "I will break." The verb shavar will come again for Jeremiah's reply and the broken bar (28:10, 13), and for the LORD's promise in 30:8. Hananiah copies the pattern of Jeremiah's own speeches: "The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says this."

a: in the fourth year, in the fifth month
p: The fourth year of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, is about the summer of 594/593 BC.
b: Zedekiah became king in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:17–18). His fourth year was 594/593 BC, and the fifth month (Ab) falls in July–August. "At the start of his reign" seems strange for the fourth year of eleven, and the Greek omits "in the same year, early in the reign" (see the variant). Some think "beginning of the reign" can mean the first part of the reign; others see the phrase as an editor's link to 27:1. Hananiah died in the seventh month (28:17), two months later.

a: Amen!
p: Was Jeremiah sincerely hoping, or speaking with irony? Readers have taken it both ways.
b: "Amen" means "let it be so." Jeremiah does not mock Hananiah at first: he says he would like it to come true, and then gives the test (28:8–9). Some read the opening as sincere, because Jeremiah suffered for his people and had no wish for disaster; others hear irony, a restrained way of saying "if only." Either way the speech does not claim that Hananiah is wrong because Jeremiah dislikes the message. Jeremiah then says nothing more until God sends a word (28:12), which is itself a sign of how a true prophet is meant to behave.

a: when that prophet's word comes true
p: Deuteronomy gave two tests, fulfillment and faithfulness to the LORD; Jeremiah adds a reason for caution.
b: Deuteronomy 18:21–22 says that if what a prophet says does not happen, he did not speak for the LORD. Deuteronomy 13:1–5 adds that a prophet whose sign does come true is still false if he calls people to other gods, so fulfillment is a necessary test but not the only one. Jeremiah 28:8–9 adds that a prophet of peace carries the greater burden of proof because earlier prophets mostly announced war and disaster. Critics note that this is not a universal rule: Isaiah and Nahum also proclaimed deliverance, and Jeremiah's own warnings were conditional (18:7–10; 26:3), so a warning that does not happen can mean the people repented. Hananiah's test was settled within two months, when he died (28:17).

a: smashed it
p: Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's sign; Jeremiah leaves and waits for a word.
b: Hananiah answers a sign-act with his own. He takes the wooden bar from Jeremiah's neck and smashes it, saying the yoke of Babylon will break the same way in two years (28:11). Neither man proves anything by action alone. Jeremiah "went his way" without replying, and the answer comes later, as a new word from the LORD (28:12–14). The contrast is the book's picture of the difference between a prophet who acts on his own hopes and one who waits for the word.

a: a yoke of iron
p: "A yoke of iron" comes from the covenant curses: the people who ignore the LORD will carry one.
b: Deuteronomy 28:48 lists among the curses for disobedience that the LORD would put "a yoke of iron on your neck" until the people were destroyed. Jeremiah changes Hananiah's broken wood into iron: a yoke that can be broken only by the one who put it on. The Plain keeps "yoke-bars" for 28:13 and "yoke" here; the Hebrew uses two nouns. The same chain returns in 30:8, when the LORD promises to break the yoke himself, in the opposite direction.

a: The LORD did not send you
p: Shalach is a pun: the LORD did not send Hananiah, so he will send him off the earth.
b: The verb shalach ("send") is the mark of a true prophet: 1:7; 26:12, 15. Hananiah was not sent (28:15), so the LORD will "send" him away from the face of the earth (28:16). The pun is sharper in Hebrew, where the two verbs are the same word in different forms. The Greek says only that Hananiah "made this people trust in an unjust thing." The charge in 28:16, "spoken rebellion against the LORD" (sarah), matches the wording of Deuteronomy 13:5, where a false prophet is to be put to death.

a: died that same year, in the seventh month
p: Two months after the contest, Hananiah dies, just as Jeremiah said.
b: The fifth month (28:1) to the seventh month (28:17) is about two months. The text states the death as the fulfillment of 28:16 and as a sign that Hananiah was not sent, not as an act by Jeremiah. Ezekiel 11:13 gives another case in which a prophet's word is followed by the death of a man named in the vision. Deuteronomy 18:20 says a prophet who speaks presumptuously must die, and the author reads Hananiah's death as the LORD's own verdict. Jewish and Christian readers have often taken the story as a lesson that the true word may be unwelcome and slow, while the false one is quick and popular.

a: the letter
t: The letter and the exiles in Babylon
p: Jeremiah's letter reached a community that was settling into Babylonian life.
b: The letter went to those carried off with Jehoiachin in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:14–16): a number given as 10,000 in 2 Kings 24:14, 8,000 in 24:16 and 3,023 in Jeremiah 52:28 (the counts differ). Cuneiform tablets from the village of Al-Yahudu ("Judah-town") in Babylonia, dated from about 572 BC on, show Judean exiles farming, renting land and keeping records, which fits the advice to build and plant (29:5). Ezekiel, among the same exiles, calls them rebels and speaks to "elders" who sat with him (Ezekiel 8:1; 14:1). The letter is one of the earliest surviving examples of a prophet writing instead of speaking.

a: the queen mother
p: The king's mother held a high office in Judah and was deported with her son.
b: The queen mother (gevirah, "great lady") of Jehoiachin was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8, 12, 15). Jeremiah had warned her and the king earlier (13:18; 22:26). Many identify her father with Elnathan son of Achbor (26:22; 36:12), though the Bible does not say so. Her fate is a sign of how far the 597 BC deportation reached: the royal family, the officials and the craftsmen and smiths that 2 Kings 24:14 names.

a: Build houses and settle in them. Plant gardens and eat what they grow.
t: Build and plant: the curse reversed
p: Under the covenant curses, a man builds a house and does not live in it; Jeremiah tells the exiles to build and live.
b: Deuteronomy 28:30 lists among the curses that you build a house and do not live in it, plant a vineyard and do not use its fruit. Jeremiah tells the exiles to do the opposite while they are still under the curse. The verbs "build" and "plant" are also half of his commission in 1:10, which ends with "to build and to plant." The instruction was costly: it meant giving up the hope of a quick return (29:28). Hananiah's promise of two years (28:3) said the opposite.

a: Seek the peace
p: Shalom means peace and also welfare; the exiles are told to work for Babylon's good.
b: Shalom covers peace, health and well-being. The same word is used three times in 29:7, and the verse says the exiles' peace is tied to the city's. The command is unusual because the exiles lived in a conquering city, and Psalm 137 shows another mood. The Greek says "land," not "city." Augustine used the verse to say that the Christian pilgrims in the earthly city may use its peace (City of God 19.26), and 1 Peter 1:1; 2:11–17 speaks of Christians as "exiles." The Mishnah records a rabbi's advice to pray for the government's welfare (Mishnah Avot 3:2). The verse is not a promise that Babylon would be spared (25:12; 50–51).

a: the dreams you are getting them to dream
p: The Hebrew form can mean the exiles cause the dreams to be dreamed, by wanting them.
b: The verb is a causative form, machlimim, "cause to dream." So the best sense is that the exiles, wanting good news, encourage the dreamers, and a prophet of the people's wishes appears. The Greek and some readers take it as "the dreams you dream." The Plain follows the Hebrew form. The idea fits Jeremiah's saying that prophets who tell people only what they want to hear are worthless (23:16–17; compare 2 Timothy 4:3).

a: seventy years for Babylon
t: How the seventy years are counted
p: Several counts fit "seventy"; the Bible itself uses the number in more than one way.
b: Jeremiah first gives the number in 25:11–12 for the time Babylon rules. Three main counts are used. From Nebuchadnezzar's rise (605 BC) to Cyrus's decree (538) is about 67 years. From the fall of the Temple (586) to its rebuilding (516) is exactly 70. Many scholars take "seventy" as a round number for a lifetime (Psalm 90:10; Isaiah 23:15). 2 Chronicles 36:21 links it to the land's Sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34–35), Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5 count seventy years of anger, and Daniel 9:2, 24 rereads the seventy as seventy weeks of years. The Greek says "when seventy years are about to be completed for Babylon."
r: Jeremiah 25:11–12; 2 Chronicles 36:21; Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 7:5; Daniel 9:2; Daniel 9:24; Leviticus 26:34–35

a: plans for peace, not for harm
p: The verse was addressed to the exiles as a people; many readers today apply it to individuals.
b: The "you" is plural, and the verse sits in a letter to the exiles. It promises that after seventy years (29:10) the exiles as a community would be brought home. It came with a long wait and a hard instruction to build, plant and pray for Babylon (29:5–7). Many preachers apply it to individuals, often as a promise of success; others warn that this strips it of its setting, since many of the adults taken in 597 BC would not live to see the return that 29:10 puts seventy years away. Careful readers keep both: the verse is about God's character and purpose toward his people, but it is not a guarantee of an easy life to any person. The Hebrew shalom in "plans for peace" means well-being, the same word as in 29:7.

a: You will look for me and find me
p: Jeremiah repeats Moses: seek the LORD with all your heart and you will find him.
b: Deuteronomy 4:29–30 and 30:1–3 promise that Israel in exile will find the LORD if they seek him "with all your heart and all your being." The verse here is a close echo, and so is 2 Chronicles 15:2, 4. The exiles, who might think the LORD stayed in Jerusalem with the Temple, are told he can be found in Babylon. The Greek of verse 14 reads "I will appear to you" and has no promise of return in that verse.

a: turn your fortunes around
p: A set phrase for restoring a people; it plays on shuv, "turn," Jeremiah's key word.
b: Shuv shevut is literally "turn back the turning" or "bring back the captivity" (KJV: "turn away your captivity"). Scholars debate whether the noun comes from "captive" or from "turn," because the phrase is used also of Job (Job 42:10) and of Sodom (Ezekiel 16:53), where nobody was in exile. The Plain follows the sense "turn (someone's) fortunes around." The word shuv is Jeremiah's pun on turning away and turning back (3:12–14; 8:4–5): when the people turn back, the LORD turns their fortunes.

a: The LORD has raised up prophets for us in Babylon
t: The exiles answer with prophets of their own
p: The exiles said they already had prophets in Babylon, and so did not need Jeremiah's letter.
b: Verse 15 is the exiles' reply to the letter so far: the LORD has given them prophets in Babylon, and these told them the stay would be short (compare 29:8–9, 21). The Hebrew word that opens the verse (ki) can be read as "because," tying 29:16–20 (the verses the Greek lacks) to this claim as the answer; the Plain sets the claim as a bare quotation. 29:21–23 names two such prophets, Ahab and Zedekiah.

a: disgusting figs
p: The people left in Jerusalem are compared to rotten figs, as in the vision of chapter 24.
b: The figs picture links this letter with chapter 24, where Jeremiah saw two baskets, one of good figs standing for the first exiles and one of bad figs for Zedekiah and those who stayed (see 24:1–10). The point for the exiles in Babylon is that the people in Jerusalem, who see the exiles as lost, are the ones facing judgment. The same three threats, sword, famine and disease, are in 24:10.

a: a thing to hiss at
p: Terror, curse, waste, hissing and disgrace: a list Jeremiah uses again and again.
b: The list uses stock words for shocked contempt, and similar chains stand in 24:9; 25:9, 18; 26:6 and Deuteronomy 28:25, 37. "Hissing" (sheriqah) is the sound of a person whistling in shock at a ruin (19:8). The Hebrew text writes "terror" in a different spelling in the written text and the reading tradition (Ketiv and Qere), with no change in meaning. The chain shows how the curses of the covenant were being applied.

a: whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire
p: Roasting is a rare punishment; Bavli Sanhedrin 93a tells a story about it.
b: The verb qalah ("roast, parch") is used elsewhere for toasting grain (Leviticus 2:14), so the punishment was a burning. Babylonian kings could burn offenders (Daniel 3:6). The Bible does not give any more details. The Talmud tells a story in which Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah were punished by Nebuchadnezzar after falsely claiming a prophet's permission for adultery with his daughter, and in which the High Priest Joshua was thrown into the fire with them and came out only singed, which the Gemara connects to Zechariah 3:2, "a brand plucked from the fire" (Bavli Sanhedrin 93a). The curse in this verse, "May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab," is of the same type as 26:6.

a: raves and plays the prophet
p: Shemaiah calls prophets "mad"; the same charge was made against Elisha's messenger.
b: The pair meshugga ("mad") and mitnabbe ("acts the prophet") shows a hostile view of ecstatic prophecy. The same word for "mad" is used by an officer about the young prophet sent to anoint Jehu (2 Kings 9:11) and in Hosea 9:7. "The stocks" (mahpekhet) is the device in which Pashhur the priest locked Jeremiah in 20:2. Shemaiah wants Zephaniah to treat Jeremiah the same way again, in effect making the Temple police responsible for silencing prophets.

a: Jehoiada the priest
p: Zephaniah, probably the "second priest," was later sent to Jeremiah by Zedekiah.
b: Jehoiada is not otherwise known; he seems to have been the chief priest or temple officer before Zephaniah. Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is called "the second priest" in 52:24 and is sent by Zedekiah to ask Jeremiah to pray (21:1; 37:3). So Zephaniah was not simply Jeremiah's enemy; he read the letter aloud to Jeremiah (29:29), which suggests he took no action on it. He was executed at Riblah after the fall (52:24–27).

a: Write down for yourself in a book all the words I have spoken to you
p: Chapters 30–31 are a small book of hope, written down at the LORD's command.
b: Jeremiah's work was often written down (36:2, 32; 51:60). Chapters 30–31, with the additions in 32–33 in some counts, are called the "Book of Consolation" or "Book of Comfort." Scholars disagree on its date. Many think the poems addressed to Israel, Ephraim and Samaria (31:2–22 especially) go back to Jeremiah's early ministry under Josiah, when he hoped for the return of the northern tribes (Bright; Thompson; Holladay). Others think the poems were reworked after 586, and that the headings about Judah were added then (Carroll). The Greek has the chapters in a different place, as chapters 37–38.

a: does a man ever give birth?
p: A man in labor is a picture of helpless terror in battle.
b: Prophets often pictured fear as labor pains: Isaiah 13:8; 21:3; Jeremiah 4:31; 6:24; 49:24; 50:43. The joke is bitter: warriors are doubled over as women are in childbirth. The speaker turns the image back at the end of the poem, where the birth-pangs become the way a new day is born (30:7).

a: a sickly yellow-green
p: Yeraqon means the color of pale green things, used for mildew and for fear.
b: Yeraqon is from yaraq, "green." It names the pale yellowish green of blighted grain (Deuteronomy 28:22; 1 Kings 8:37) and here the color of faces drained by terror. English "pale" would lose the color, so the Plain uses the Hebrew's picture.

a: It is a season of anguish for Jacob
p: Is Jacob's time of anguish the exile, the fall of Jerusalem or a future tribulation?
b: The Hebrew says "a time of distress it is for Jacob, and out of it he will be saved." Historical readers apply it to the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, followed by the return. Some Jewish and Christian readers link it with Daniel 12:1, a time of distress before deliverance. Dispensationalist writers identify "the time of Jacob's trouble" with the future tribulation (Daniel 9:27; 12:1; Matthew 24:21) and the rescue with the coming of the Messiah (Walvoord; Pentecost). Amillennial Christians see it fulfilled in the exile and, for the church, in Christ. All agree on the key words: the trouble is real, and it is not the end.

a: I will break his yoke off your neck
p: Hananiah said "I will break the yoke" in 28:2; the same promise is here, but with a different timetable.
b: Hananiah's sentence in 28:2, 4, 11 uses the same Hebrew verb for "break" and the same noun, "the yoke of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah's Book of Consolation now promises that the LORD will break the yoke, and the straps of 27:2 will be torn apart. The difference is when and how: not in two years and not as a reason to resist Babylon, but "on that day," after judgment, by the LORD's own act. The echo is likely intended by the book's arrangement, since chapters 27–28 and 30–31 stand next to each other.

a: David their king
p: A later king from David's line, a resurrected David, or the Messiah: readers have taken it all three ways.
b: The phrase also appears in Hosea 3:5 and Ezekiel 34:23–24; 37:24–25, and Jeremiah has the matching promise of a righteous Branch (23:5–6; 33:15–17). Most scholars read "David" as a ruler from his line, as in Ezekiel's "my servant David," not David himself. Jewish tradition read it of the Messiah: the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets has "they will obey Messiah the son of David, their king, whom I will raise up for them." Christian readers see Jesus (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30). Some read it of David raised from the dead. The promise rests on the covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
r: Hosea 3:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24; Ezekiel 37:24–25; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Jeremiah 33:15–17; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30

a: I will discipline you fairly
p: The LORD's punishment is measured; Jeremiah's own prayer asked for the same (10:24).
b: Mishpat means "justice" or "fair measure." In 10:24 Jeremiah had prayed, "Correct me, LORD, but by what is just." The same words stand in 46:28. The promise has two sides: the nations that scattered Israel will be finished off, but Israel will not be, though it will not simply be let off.

a: I will make new skin grow for you
p: Arukhah means new flesh over a wound; 30:17 answers the question of 8:22.
b: Arukhah is the new flesh that grows over a wound. In 8:22 the prophet asked why the "healing" of his people had not come up; here the LORD says he will make it come up. The verb "go up" (alah) is the same in both, and 33:6 uses the word again. In 30:13 the Plain says "no remedy" for the same te'alah, so that the "new flesh" of 30:17 is heard as the answer to it. The image of a nation as a wounded body runs through 30:12–15 and then reverses.

a: All your lovers
p: Judah's foreign allies are her "lovers," who left her when she was struck.
b: Prophets often used the language of adultery for political alliances: Hosea 2:5–13; Ezekiel 16:33–37; 23:5–10; Lamentations 1:2, 19. In Jeremiah's own words they "despise" her (4:30). The allies here are Egypt and the neighboring states that promised help against Babylon (2:36–37; 27:3). The image links to the shame of 3:1–5.

a: no one cares about her
p: The Hebrew says "no one seeks her"; Isaiah 62:12 gives her the opposite name.
b: The verb is darash, "seek, ask after, care for." Zion is described as one whom nobody looks for. Isaiah 62:12 gives her a new name meaning "sought out," which seems to answer this line. Qumran copy 4QJer-c (4Q72) writes the word "outcast" (nidachat) with a final taw where the Masoretic text has a final he, a difference in spelling the feminine ending.

a: His leader will be one of his own
p: After foreign masters (30:8), a ruler from among the people themselves.
b: Deuteronomy 17:15 required that the king be "from among your brothers," not a foreigner. The promise sets this against the foreign "strangers" of 30:8. The ruler "comes near" to the LORD, language used of priests (Exodus 24:2; Numbers 16:5), which has led some to see a priestly king, as in Zechariah 6:13 and Psalm 110. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c preserves most of the verse and agrees with the Hebrew.

a: who would put his own heart on the line
p: The verb arav means to pledge or give as security; the question is whether anyone dares.
b: Arav means "to pledge, guarantee" (Proverbs 20:16; Genesis 43:9). The Hebrew asks, "Who is this who has pledged his heart to approach me?" The sense is that coming near to God is dangerous, since only he can make anyone fit for it. Older versions say "engaged his heart." The Greek says the same thing with different wording: "who is this who has given his heart to turn to me?"

a: I will be your God
p: "You will be my people, and I will be your God" is the heart of the covenant, repeated across the Bible.
b: The formula first appears in Exodus 6:7 and Leviticus 26:12 and is repeated in Jeremiah 7:23; 11:4; 24:7; 30:22; 31:1, 33; 32:38, in Ezekiel 36:28 and, as a promise for the future, in Hosea 2:23 and Revelation 21:3. It marks both the Sinai covenant and the new covenant. The Greek lacks this verse in chapter 30 but has the formula at 31:1 and 31:33.
r: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 7:23; Jeremiah 31:33; Jeremiah 32:38; Ezekiel 36:28; Revelation 21:3

a: Fury has gone out
t: The same storm as in Jeremiah 23:19
p: 30:23–24 repeats 23:19–20 almost word for word.
b: Jeremiah 23:19–20 and 30:23–24 are the same Hebrew apart from small differences (two in 30:23, named here, and two in 30:24, named there), and the Plain gives them the same English where the Hebrew is the same. In 30:23 the storm is mitgorer (a root that can mean "whirl" or "drag, sweep") where 23:19 has mitholel ("whirling"), and 30:23 lacks a joining "and" before "storm." Both verses use the wording "burst on the heads of the wicked" and end with the plans of the LORD's heart, understood "in the last days." In 23:19–20 the words are aimed at the false prophets; in the Book of Consolation they stand at the end of the poem of Jacob's wound and speak against those who have harmed Israel.

a: In the last days
p: Acharit hayamim: a phrase for the future that ranges from "later" to "the end."
b: Acharit hayamim means "the end of the days" or "in later days." It can mean any future time (Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14) or the great age of God's reign (Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14). Jeremiah uses it also for the restoration of Moab and Elam (48:47; 49:39). Here the "understanding" may come when the events show that the storm had a purpose. This verse repeats 23:20 almost word for word; see there for the setting of the original. The two differences in the Hebrew: 30:24 has 'burning anger' (charon af) where 23:20 has only 'anger', and it stops at 'understand it' where 23:20 ends 'understand it fully' (binah).

a: A people who survived the sword
t: The wilderness as the first love
p: Hosea and Jeremiah both remember the wilderness as a time of closeness between the LORD and Israel.
b: The "survivors of the sword" can be the Exodus generation who survived Amalek and other attacks (Exodus 17:8–16), or the survivors of the Assyrian conquest and the exile, for whom the way home is a second wilderness walk. Hosea 2:14–15 and 9:10 and Jeremiah 2:2–3 speak of the wilderness as the honeymoon. The Hebrew continues "when I went to bring him rest," or "as Israel went to find rest," and the sentence can be taken in either way. The Greek text has quite different wording (see the variant), while the Qumran copy 4QJer-c preserves "found favor in the wilderness" as in the Hebrew.

a: a love that lasts forever
p: The LORD's love is not new or tied to Israel's behavior.
b: Ahavat olam, "love of long ages," is spoken here to Israel as a whole, in the singular. It explains why the LORD continues to act: not because of merit but because of his own love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Isaiah 54:8; Hosea 11:1–4). The phrase became the name of the blessing before the Shema in the Jewish evening prayer, Ahavat Olam. Jeremiah 31:3 is also the verse Christians often quote when speaking of God's love for the world, though in context it is addressed to Israel.

a: kept drawing you with loyal love
p: Mashakh can mean "draw" or "prolong"; both fit hesed, the LORD's loyal love.
b: The verb mashakh means "to draw, drag" and also "to extend" or "to continue." The Hebrew says either "I have drawn you with loyal love" (compare Hosea 11:4, "cords of kindness") or "I have continued loyal love to you" (compare Psalm 36:10). The Plain's "kept drawing" holds both senses. Hesed is the loyal love that belongs to a covenant.

a: virgin Israel
p: Betulah is a title for a nation or city in its unspoiled youth; it does not describe the people's past.
b: Betulah usually means a young woman of marriageable age who is presumed to be a virgin. "Virgin Israel" and "virgin Judah" are poetic titles (Amos 5:2; Lamentations 1:15; Jeremiah 18:13; 31:21). The title does not say Israel was faithful: it promises a fresh start. The tambourine (tof) was the instrument of women's victory dances (Exodus 15:20; Judges 11:34).

a: put the fruit to everyday use
p: The Hebrew verb for "use" comes from the law about fruit trees.
b: Chillel here means "treat as ordinary," in the sense of the rule that a new orchard's fruit was off limits for three years, holy in the fourth, and could be eaten in the fifth (Leviticus 19:23–25; Deuteronomy 20:6). The promise is that the vineyards on the hills of Samaria will be planted and the owners will live to enjoy them. It reverses the curse that someone else would eat the fruit (Deuteronomy 28:30).

a: Ephraim's hill country
p: The poem imagines the north, split off for 300 years, joining Jerusalem's worship again.
b: After Solomon's death the northern tribes set up shrines at Bethel and Dan so that their people would not go to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26–33). Assyria destroyed the kingdom in 722/721 BC and carried many people away. This poem promises a day when watchmen in Ephraim's hill country call the pilgrims to go to Zion. Josiah's reform extended into the old northern territory (2 Kings 23:15–20), which is one reason many scholars date the core of these poems to his reign.

a: at the head of the nations
p: Israel is called the head of the nations, as in the promise of Deuteronomy 28:13.
b: The Hebrew rosh haggoyim is "head of the nations"; the singing is to be loud, as for a victor. Deuteronomy 28:1, 13 promised that obedient Israel would be the head, not the tail. The poem uses the language of triumph for a people who are still captives. The word "remnant" (she'erit) at the end of the verse looks forward to the survivors who return.

a: the land of the north
p: Babylon lay east, but its armies came in from the north, and the return is from "the north" too.
b: Jeremiah often calls the place of exile "the north": 3:18; 16:14–15; 23:7–8; 31:8. The foe in chapters 4–6 also comes "from the north" (4:6; 6:22). The expression pictures a second exodus, in which the LORD gathers his people from the farthest corners of the earth. The mention of the pregnant woman and those in labor shows that no one is left behind.

a: streams of water
t: The way home is a new Exodus
p: A straight road with water along it recalls the Exodus and Isaiah's highway.
b: Isaiah 35:8–10 and 40:3–4 describe a level highway through the wilderness for the returning exiles, with streams where there was desert (Isaiah 41:18; 43:19). Here the LORD himself leads them as a father. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c reads al ("by, beside") where the Masoretic text has el ("to"), and the Greek has epi as well (see the variant); the sense of the line is much the same. "Weeping" is the sign of repentance rather than sorrow only, since the next line speaks of prayers for mercy.

a: Ephraim is my firstborn
p: Israel is the LORD's firstborn in Exodus 4:22; here the name is Ephraim, the leading northern tribe.
b: Exodus 4:22 calls Israel "my firstborn son." Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, who received the first blessing from Jacob (Genesis 48:13–20) and became the head of the northern kingdom. Hosea 11:1–4, 8–9 speaks in the same way of the LORD as father to Ephraim. Calling God "father" is rare in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8; Malachi 2:10), which makes this verse stand out.

a: the islands far away
p: The Hebrew iyyim means coastlands or islands, the far edge of the known world.
b: Iyyim ("islands, coastlands") names the far west, across the Mediterranean (Isaiah 41:1; 42:4, 10; 49:1). The call goes out not only to Israel but to the nations, so that the whole world hears that the scattered people will be gathered. The Plain renders the word "the islands" everywhere.

a: as a shepherd watches his flock
p: The LORD as shepherd is a picture used of kings and of God.
b: The ancient Near East called kings shepherds, and the Bible uses it for the LORD himself in Psalm 23:1; 80:1; Isaiah 40:11; Ezekiel 34:11–16. Jeremiah condemns the "shepherds" who scattered the sheep (23:1–4) and promises the LORD will gather them. John 10:11 takes up the image for Jesus.

a: ransomed Jacob
p: Pada and ga'al are the two Exodus words for buying someone's freedom.
b: Pada ("ransom") and ga'al ("redeem") are used of the Exodus (Deuteronomy 7:8; 15:15; Exodus 6:6; 15:13), and Isaiah uses both for the return from Babylon (Isaiah 43:1; 44:22–23; 51:11). The redeemer (go'el) is normally a family member who buys back a relative (Ruth 4:4–6). The language says that the LORD owns Israel as his own family and has the right and the will to rescue her from "a hand too strong for him." In the northern poem of 31:2–22 that hand is Assyria, which ended the kingdom of Israel in 722/721 BC; for the exiles who read the finished book it was Babylon.

a: stream to the LORD's good gifts
p: Nahar can mean "flow" or "be bright"; the Plain keeps the stream picture.
b: Nahar means "flow, stream" (Isaiah 2:2; Jeremiah 51:44) and also, from another root, "be radiant, shine" (Isaiah 60:5; Psalm 34:5). Both meanings suit a joyful crowd. The Plain follows the first because the next words ("to the grain, the new wine...") name the goal of a procession. The Qumran copy 4QJer-c reads al ("over, to") instead of el ("to"), and the Greek has ep' in the same place ("they will come to the LORD's good things," Greek 38:12); see the variant. Hebrew al would fit "shine over" as well as "stream to," and the three al phrases that follow (grain, wine, oil) read the same way. The three crops, grain, wine and oil, were the staples of the land.

a: soak the priests with rich food
p: Deshen means fat or richness; the priests lived on the portions of the sacrifices.
b: Deshen means "fat" and so "richness, abundance." The priests received portions of the offerings (Deuteronomy 18:1–5). The verse pictures a time of abundant sacrifice and food, when the altar is busy and the priests are well fed. The Greek says "the sons of Levi" after "priests."

a: A voice is heard in Ramah
t: Rachel weeping, then and in Matthew
p: Rachel, mother of the northern tribes, weeps for her exiled children; Matthew hears the same grief at Bethlehem.
b: Rachel was the mother of Joseph (so of Ephraim and Manasseh) and Benjamin. Ramah in Benjamin was a gathering point for the captives: in 40:1 the Babylonian commander released Jeremiah there from a line of chained exiles. Rachel's tomb is placed near Bethlehem in Genesis 35:16–20 and in Benjamin's territory in 1 Samuel 10:2, which is one reason Matthew can link her grief to Bethlehem (Matthew 2:17–18). Matthew does not say Jeremiah predicted Herod's killing of the children; he says "was fulfilled," a word he uses for patterns in which Israel's history recurs. Readers differ whether it is typology (the exile pattern repeats), a prophecy (a direct forecast) or a reuse of familiar words. In the Hebrew the last word is singular, "because he is not."

a: Turn me back, and I will turn back
p: Ephraim asks God to turn him; the next line says he will then turn. Grace comes first.
b: Hashiveni ve'ashuvah is "cause me to turn back, and I will turn back," the key pun of the book (3:12–14, 22; 8:4–5). Lamentations 5:21 has the same shape: bring us back to you, LORD, and we will turn back. Jeremiah 3:22 gave the call and the answer in the same words of turning. The prayer confesses that repentance itself is a gift. Ephraim also admits being like an untrained calf.

a: I slapped my thigh
p: Slapping the thigh was a sign of distress, remorse or deep shock.
b: Ezekiel 21:12 tells the prophet to "strike your thigh" as a sign of grief, and the same gesture is used in Jeremiah 31:19. The gesture is not a sign of anger but of mourning for one's own folly. Ephraim says he has "borne the disgrace of my youth": the shame that follows from his early rebellion (3:24–25). The Greek says he "groaned."

a: my insides churn for him
p: The Hebrew uses the body (me'im, insides) and the word for mercy, which comes from the womb.
b: Me'im means "inner parts" or "bowels," the seat of deep feeling. The verb for "have mercy" (racham) is related to rechem, "womb." Hosea 11:8 gives the same movement of the LORD's heart: "My heart turns over within me." The verse has the LORD speaking against Ephraim and then finding that he cannot stop remembering him. For readers of the New Testament it can sound like the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:20).

a: the road you went by
p: The written Hebrew says "I went"; the reading tradition says "you went."
b: The consonants of the Leningrad Codex read halakhti, "I went" (Ketiv), and the margin tells the reader to say halakht, "you went" (Qere). The Plain follows the Qere because the verse is addressed to virgin Israel, who is told to set up signposts for the road she took into exile. The scroll 4QJer-c has the word only in restored letters, so it cannot decide.

a: a woman will surround a man
p: One of the hardest lines in the book; four main readings, each with some support.
b: The Hebrew is neqevah tesovev gaver. (1) Radak (and Rashi in part) read it as a reversal of the usual courtship: Israel the woman will go after her God the man, as the new thing (Rashi on 31:22; Radak on 31:22, who says the people themselves will turn back to seek the LORD, both as read on Sefaria). (2) Some modern scholars take it as a woman protecting a man, a reversal of roles in war. (3) Others read "a female will court a strong man" (as in Song of Songs 3:2). (4) Early Christian writers applied it to Mary carrying Christ in her womb (Jerome's commentary discusses this reading). The verb sabab means "go around, surround." The Greek has no such line, reading "salvation" for a new planting (see the variant). The Qumran copy breaks off at the key words.

a: At this I woke up and looked around
p: Jeremiah wakes as if from a dream; he elsewhere dismisses false prophets' dreams.
b: The speaker is most likely Jeremiah, saying that the hopeful vision of 31:2–25 came to him in sleep. This sits oddly with 23:25–28, where he scorns prophets who tell their dreams, though that passage condemns those who tell dreams in place of the LORD's word and not all dreams. Other readers see a gloss, an editor's comment that the hopeful poems were a pleasure to read. Another suggestion is that the sweet sleep means the end of the people's long "sleep" of exile. Daniel 7:1 and Zechariah 4:1 use waking from a vision in a similar way.

a: I will sow seed in the house of Israel
p: The LORD sows people and animals, as in Hosea's "Jezreel," which means "God sows."
b: Hosea 2:22–23 plays on the name Jezreel ("God sows"): the LORD will sow Israel in the land. Ezekiel 36:9–11 promises that the land will be sown and people and animals multiplied. The pairing of people and animals recalls the land's devastation in Jeremiah 7:20 and 32:43, now reversed.

a: I watched over them
p: The verb shaqad is the one in the almond-branch vision of chapter 1.
b: The verb is shaqad, "to watch, be wakeful." In 1:11–12 Jeremiah saw a branch of the almond tree (shaqed) and heard the LORD say he was watching (shoqed) over his word. Here the same watching is applied to both uprooting and building. The Plain gives the verbs of destruction the same English as 1:10 ("pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish"): the list in this verse is "pull up, pull down, demolish, destroy, bring harm," one verb more than 1:10.

a: to build and to plant
p: The second half of Jeremiah's commission, now about to come true.
b: "To build and to plant" completes the commission of 1:10, and the same pair is used in 18:9; 24:6; 42:10 and 45:4. For the exiles it is the program of 29:5. The LORD both tears down and builds, and the book holds the two together.

a: The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb
p: People blamed their parents for their troubles; Jeremiah and Ezekiel both answer.
b: The saying means that parents' sins fall on the children. It may reflect Exodus 20:5, and Lamentations 5:7 uses a similar thought. It can also be an excuse: "it isn't our fault." Ezekiel 18:2–4 quotes the same proverb to refute it and teach individual responsibility. Jeremiah's line looks to a future time: each person will die for his own guilt (compare Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Kings 14:6). Yet Jeremiah 32:18 speaks of the LORD repaying the fathers' guilt into the lap of their children. The tension is real; readers reconcile it by seeing family consequences in life and personal accountability before God.

a: I will cut a new covenant
p: The only use of "new covenant" in the Old Testament; to "cut" a covenant means to seal it with a sacrifice.
b: Berit chadashah occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. "Cut" (karat) comes from the old rite of cutting animals to seal an agreement (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18). The Qumran community called itself "the new covenant in the land of Damascus" (Damascus Document CD VI, 19). In the New Testament, Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 have Jesus say "the new covenant in my blood," while Matthew 26:28 and Mark 14:24 (in the best manuscripts) speak of his blood of the covenant, words that recall Exodus 24:8. 2 Corinthians 3:6 and Hebrews 8:8–13; 10:16–17 quote or use Jeremiah. "New" may mean "renewed" and not "replacing."
r: Genesis 15:9–18; Exodus 24:8; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Hebrews 8:8–13; Hebrews 10:16–17

a: the house of Israel and with the house of Judah
p: The promise names Israel and Judah, the divided kingdoms, now reunited.
b: The covenant is promised to the "house of Israel" and the "house of Judah," the northern and southern kingdoms, both. Hebrews 8:8 repeats the names. Jewish readers take the promise as made to the Jewish people; most Christian traditions say it is fulfilled in Christ and extended to Gentiles who are in him; dispensationalists say it will be fulfilled with national Israel in the future; Messianic Jewish writers say it is for the Jewish people through Yeshua. The views are set side by side in the "Where Christians differ" card for this chapter. Radak understood it to mean that Israel will keep the covenant this time.

a: They broke that covenant of mine
p: The Sinai covenant failed because the people broke it, not because it was bad.
b: Hefer ("break, annul") is the covenant-breaking verb (Genesis 17:14; Leviticus 26:15; Jeremiah 11:10; Ezekiel 16:59). The new covenant is not described as a better law but as one that will be kept, because of what the LORD does inside people (31:33). Hebrews 8:7–9 draws the conclusion that the first covenant was faulty "with the people," and Radak reads it as a promise that Israel will keep the same Torah.

a: and on their hearts I will write it
p: The law moves from stone tablets to the center of the will.
b: At Sinai God wrote on stone (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10). Jeremiah had said earlier that Judah's sin was written on the tablet of the heart with an iron pen (17:1). Now the LORD writes his law there. In the Bible the "heart" is the mind and will together. Deuteronomy 30:6, 14 and Ezekiel 36:26–27 give related promises, and Paul in 2 Corinthians 3:3 says the Corinthians are a letter written "on tablets that are hearts of flesh." Jewish readers (Radak) stress that the Torah is the same one, now kept; Christian readers see the Spirit's work.
r: Exodus 31:18; Jeremiah 17:1; Deuteronomy 30:6; Ezekiel 36:26–27; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Hebrews 10:16

a: They will not teach any more
t: Does everyone really know the LORD?
p: Teaching goes on in the New Testament, so the promise is about knowing, not the end of instruction.
b: "They will all know me" does not end teaching: Deuteronomy 6:7 and the New Testament itself (Matthew 28:20; Hebrews 5:12) keep it. Readers have taken it to mean that teaching will no longer need to say "Know the LORD" to people who do not know him, or that knowledge of God will no longer depend on a priestly class, or that it describes the final state. 1 John 2:20, 27 says believers have an anointing and "have no need that anyone teach you." Baptists and others argue that the verse limits the new covenant community to people who actually know God, which leads to the baptism question on the card for this chapter. "Know" (yada) is a word for faithful relationship (Hosea 4:1; 6:6), not just information.

a: their sin I will remember no more
p: In the Bible, to remember is to act on something; to forget is to stop holding it against someone.
b: The Hebrew zakhar, "remember," often means to take notice and act (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24). "I will remember their sin no more" is therefore a promise that the LORD will not act on it, and not a claim that he loses the memory. Compare Isaiah 43:25; Psalm 103:12; Micah 7:19. Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17 quote this line to say the sacrifice of Christ ends the need for repeated offerings. In Jewish thought it is tied to the forgiveness the LORD gives on the Day of Atonement.

a: rules for the moon and stars
p: Sun, moon and stars keep fixed rules; Israel's existence is said to be as secure.
b: Chuqqot are fixed rules or decrees, here the laws of nature, the pattern God set (Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 148:6; Job 38:33). Jeremiah 33:20, 25 uses the same idea as the "covenant with day and night" (the Greek lacks chapter 33:14–26). The argument is that Israel's place in God's plan is as dependable as the sun.

a: the offspring of Israel too will stop
p: This is the main Old Testament text for Israel's permanence as a nation, used by Jews and Christians.
b: The conditional statement means that Israel will be a nation as long as the sun and moon keep their order, and the sun and moon are not going to change. Jewish readers see it as a promise that the Jewish people will never disappear. Christians have used it in the debate over the church and Israel: those who hold that God still has a plan for the Jewish people cite it with Romans 11:1–2, 29, while others read "Israel" as the people of God, including the church (Galatians 6:16). The contrast with Hosea 1:9 is also noted.

a: from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate
t: The boundaries of the new Jerusalem
p: The line runs from the northeast corner of the old city around to the northwest.
b: The Tower of Hananel stood at the north side of the Temple area (Nehemiah 3:1; 12:39; Zechariah 14:10) and the Corner Gate at the northwest (2 Kings 14:13; Zechariah 14:10). Gareb and Goah are otherwise unknown, so the circuit cannot be traced fully. The description has been compared with Nehemiah's building of the wall (Nehemiah 3), which some see as a first fulfillment, and with the visions of Ezekiel 40–48 and Revelation 21.
r: Nehemiah 3:1; Nehemiah 12:39; Zechariah 14:10; 2 Kings 14:13; Ezekiel 40–48; Revelation 21:2

a: valley of the corpses and the fat ashes
t: A burial and ash ground made holy
p: The place of death and waste is to be set apart for the LORD.
b: The "valley of corpses" is usually identified with the Valley of Hinnom or the Kidron, south and east of the city, where bodies and Temple ash were dumped. Jeremiah 7:31–33 and 19:6–13 had called the Valley of Hinnom the place of slaughter. "Fat ashes" are the ashes of the altar fat (Leviticus 1:16; 6:10–11). To say that this ground will be "holy to the LORD" is to say that even the unclean places will be part of the city. The Hebrew text has a Ketiv/Qere difference for "fields" (terraced fields, sheremot, in the written text; fields, shedemot, in the reading).

a: pulled up or demolished
p: Jerusalem was torn down again in AD 70, so readers differ on what "never again" means.
b: The Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 and again after the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132–135), so the promise cannot be about the city in Nehemiah's day. Jewish readers keep it as a hope for the restored Jerusalem; many Christians read it of the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2) or of the church; dispensationalists expect a literal rebuilt Jerusalem in the age to come. The verbs here, "pull up" and "demolish," are verbs of Jeremiah's commission (1:10; 31:28), so the promise returns to the book's first words.
